analysis.title: Copper: priced for AI perfection
key_insights: Copper's structural story remains compelling but near-term risk/reward has shifted. Prices reflect strong AI investment and also the timely delivery of a very large global data-centre construction pipeline.

Data centres are estimated to add around 350kt to copper demand in 2026, from essentially nothing as recently as 2023. Annual copper consumption is roughly 28mt, so the contribution is still modest but growing quickly.
Combined 2026 capex guidance from Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta is around USD720-745bn, up from roughly USD410bn in 2025. Their Q2 cash capex reached USD165bn, up 87% y/y.
BloombergNEF estimates installed US data-centre capacity could reach 194GW by 2035, 83% above its December 2025 forecast. The speed of these revisions is a reason for caution.
Copper's performance has increasingly mirrored AI-related equities, so copper is exposed to expectations for future data-centre construction as well as today's physical demand.

Kpler estimates 2026 data-centre construction could require 300-700kt of copper, with grid reinforcement requiring a further 300-500kt. Not all grid spending is incremental AI demand because some serves wider electrification.
ANZ forecasts 2026 mine supply growth of only 1.2% y/y and a market deficit of around 323kt. Large mines take years to approve and develop, so supply responds slowly to demand.

Demand from projects under construction is relatively secure. The uncertainty is in the much larger prospective pipeline, which makes copper sensitive to the scale, timing and completion rate of future projects.

Community opposition is building. A proposed West Footscray facility in Australia met opposition over construction disruption, noise and diesel emissions, and its power infrastructure was delayed. Victoria tightened rules, including 150-metre buffers around homes and schools.

US voters considered 41 local data-centre ballot measures across 10 states around the 2026 midterms. Restrictions won or pro-development measures failed in almost every contest with results available, and voters rebuffed data centres in all but one ballot.

Texas could account for about 25-30% of US data-centre capacity expected online by 2030. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a temporary halt to new construction, and the previous administration had suspended approvals over grid concerns.

Georgia Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms campaigned on pausing new data-centre construction and said she intends to pursue an immediate pause. A federal Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act has been introduced.

ANZ treats a nationwide moratorium as a tail risk. The more plausible threat is that state and local permitting, grid connection and planning make approvals harder, raise costs and push completion dates out.

ANZ frames three tests for AI copper demand: returns (do hyperscalers still want to build), infrastructure (can they build) and social licence (will they be allowed to build). AI computing demand can keep rising even if the physical build-out slows.
Infrastructure bottlenecks support copper while they trigger extra grid spending, but beyond a point they delay commissioning and become a constraint.
Traditional copper demand is mixed, and high prices encourage substitution, thrifting and scrap use, which makes AI-related consumption more important at the margin.

Scenarios: bull (AI investment accelerates, deficit widens, further upside), base (growth slows, projects delayed not destroyed, prices elevated but volatile), bear (pipeline cut, near-term balance loosens, sharp cyclical correction).

Every 10GW removed from the pipeline would cut gross facility-level copper demand by roughly 270-450kt, before timing, substitution, recycling or grid investment. The Chicago benchmark is 27t/MW, and AI-intensive facilities could need 30-45t/MW.

ANZ sees the principal downside risk as a cyclical correction within a structural bull market. Copper needs only for the future to arrive more slowly than expected for prices to come under pressure, not for the AI boom to collapse.
ANZ expects the copper market to enter a structural deficit because investment in mine and recycling capacity lags demand.

sector_views.rationale: Structural story intact, but prices embed aggressive AI data-centre build-out, so the bar for upside surprises is high and the principal risk is a cyclical correction.

macro_indicators.interpretation: ANZ's forecast of a tight market with mine supply growth of only 1.2% y/y supports prices, but a delayed data-centre pipeline could push expected deficits further out.
Small against about 28mt annual consumption but growing fast, and it drives investor expectations for future copper demand.
Guidance up from roughly USD410bn in 2025. It underpins copper demand expectations, but only the part converted into physical infrastructure counts.

risk_factors: Hyperscalers cut uncommitted projects if returns on AI spending deteriorate.
Power, transmission, transformer, water and land constraints delay data-centre commissioning.
Community opposition and state or local political action make approvals harder and raise costs.
A federal data-centre moratorium, which ANZ calls a tail risk.
High prices encourage substitution, thrifting and scrap use, while traditional demand is mixed.
Forecast pipeline estimates may be inflated, as BloombergNEF's 2035 capacity forecast rose 83% in under a year.
vol_and_positioning: Copper's performance has increasingly mirrored AI-related equities, so a pullback in AI stocks transmits to copper. Recent weakness in AI equities shows investors questioning returns on AI spending.
geopolitical: Local and state political opposition to data centres in the US, including Texas and Georgia governor-elects campaigning on construction pauses and a proposed federal Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act.
Community opposition and tighter data-centre rules in Victoria, Australia.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscaler capex of USD720-745bn in 2026 and a 194GW US capacity pipeline by 2035 add a demand engine against mine supply growth of only 1.2% y/y and a deficit of about 323kt. Power bottlenecks that trigger grid investment also add copper demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Weak AI returns, power and permitting constraints and political opposition (41 local ballot measures, Texas and Georgia pauses) could delay or cancel the pipeline and push expected deficits further out, causing a sharp cyclical correction in expectations-driven prices.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence of delays or cancellations in the data-centre pipeline, such as state-level construction pauses or hyperscalers cutting uncommitted projects, would undermine the bull case. Construction above already ambitious forecasts would invalidate the bear case.

theme_stances.key_argument: Copper prices embed aggressive data-centre build-out, so delays alone could trigger a cyclical correction within a structural bull market.
theme_stances.evidence: Copper doesn't need the AI boom to collapse for prices

theme_stances.key_argument: State and local permitting, grid connection and planning decisions can delay data centres without a national ban.
theme_stances.evidence: approvals become more difficult, development costs rise
